cases.title: Acute Chest Pain in Middle-Aged Man
learning_objectives: Differentiate acute coronary syndrome from other causes of chest pain
Apply HEART score for risk stratification
cases.presentation: 55-year-old man with sudden-onset crushing chest pain radiating to left arm, associated with diaphoresis and dyspnea

history.chief_complaint: Chest pain for 1 hour
history.hpi: Patient was mowing lawn when developed severe substernal chest pressure. Pain radiates to left arm and jaw. Associated with shortness of breath and sweating. No relief with rest.
history.social: Smoking 1 PPD x 30 years, occasional alcohol

labs.ecg: ST elevation in leads II, III, aVF

cases.explanation: This is a classic presentation of inferior STEMI. Key features include: (1) Cardiac risk factors (smoking, HTN, DM, HLD, family history), (2) Classic anginal chest pain with radiation, (3) Associated symptoms (diaphoresis, dyspnea), (4) Elevated troponin, (5) ST elevation in inferior leads (II, III, aVF). Time is muscle - activate cath lab immediately!
management_pearls: MONA: Morphine, Oxygen (if hypoxic), Nitroglycerin, Aspirin 325mg
Activate cath lab for emergent PCI (door-to-balloon <90 min)
Dual antiplatelet therapy: Aspirin + P2Y12 inhibitor (ticagrelor or prasugrel)
Anticoagulation: Heparin or bivalirudin
Beta-blocker and ACE inhibitor within 24 hours
High-intensity statin (atorvastatin 80mg)

cases.title: Young Woman with Severe Headache
learning_objectives: Recognize red flags for secondary headache
cases.presentation: 28-year-old woman with sudden-onset 'worst headache of life', associated with neck stiffness and photophobia

history.chief_complaint: Severe headache for 2 hours
history.hpi: Patient was at work when suddenly developed explosive headache. Describes it as 'thunderclap' - reached maximum intensity within seconds. Associated with nausea, vomiting, and neck pain. No trauma.
history.pmh: Migraine headaches (different character), no previous similar episodes
history.social: Non-smoker, social drinker

physical_exam.neuro: Alert and oriented, cranial nerves intact, no focal deficits

imaging.lp: Opening pressure 25 cm H2O, RBC 50,000 (tube 1) and 48,000 (tube 4), xanthochromia present

cases.explanation: Classic subarachnoid hemorrhage presentation: 'thunderclap headache' (sudden, severe, maximal at onset), meningismus (neck stiffness), photophobia. CT shows blood in basilar cisterns. LP confirms SAH with persistent RBCs and xanthochromia (breakdown of hemoglobin). Key is recognizing 'worst headache of life' red flag.
management_pearls: Immediate neurosurgery consult
CT angiography to identify aneurysm source
Nimodipine 60mg q4h to prevent vasospasm
Blood pressure control: SBP <160 mmHg (avoid hypotension)
Serial neuro exams for deterioration
Prevent rebleeding: early aneurysm securement (coiling or clipping)

cases.title: Elderly Man with Fever and Productive Cough
learning_objectives: Apply CURB-65 score for severity assessment
cases.presentation: 72-year-old man with 3 days of fever, productive cough with green sputum, and shortness of breath

history.chief_complaint: Cough and fever for 3 days
history.hpi: Patient developed fever, chills, and productive cough 3 days ago. Sputum is green-yellow. Associated with pleuritic chest pain on right side. Progressive dyspnea.
history.social: Former smoker (quit 5 years ago), 40 pack-year history

physical_exam.lungs: Decreased breath sounds right lower lobe, crackles, egophony

cases.explanation: Community-acquired pneumonia with typical presentation: fever, productive cough, pleuritic chest pain, hypoxia, tachypnea. Physical exam shows focal findings (crackles, egophony). CXR confirms consolidation. CURB-65 score: 2 points (age >65, elevated BUN) suggests moderate severity requiring hospitalization.
management_pearls: CURB-65: Confusion, Urea >7 mmol/L, RR ≥30, BP <90/60, age ≥65
Empiric antibiotics: Ceftriaxone + azithromycin or respiratory fluoroquinolone
Supplemental oxygen to maintain SpO2 >90%
IV fluids for hydration
Blood cultures before antibiotics
Consider MRSA/Pseudomonas coverage if risk factors present
references: Community-Acquired Pneumonia in Adults: Diagnosis and Management

cases.title: Young Adult with Abdominal Pain
learning_objectives: Differentiate surgical vs non-surgical acute abdomen
cases.presentation: 22-year-old man with 12 hours of progressive right lower quadrant abdominal pain, nausea, and fever

history.chief_complaint: Belly pain for 12 hours
history.hpi: Pain started periumbilically this morning, then migrated to RLQ. Worsening over time. Associated with anorexia, nausea, one episode of vomiting. No diarrhea. Pain worse with movement.
history.social: College student, occasional alcohol

physical_exam.abdomen: RLQ tenderness maximal at McBurney's point, rebound and guarding present, positive Rovsing's sign

imaging.ct_abdomen: Dilated appendix 12mm with periappendiceal fat stranding

cases.explanation: Classic acute appendicitis: periumbilical pain migrating to RLQ, anorexia, fever, leukocytosis. Physical exam findings (McBurney's point tenderness, rebound, guarding, Rovsing's sign) strongly suggest appendicitis. CT confirms diagnosis. Alvarado score ≥7 indicates high probability requiring surgical consultation.
management_pearls: NPO and IV fluids for resuscitation
Antibiotics: Ceftriaxone + metronidazole or piperacillin-tazobactam
Pain control: IV opioids after surgical evaluation
Urgent surgical consultation for appendectomy
Laparoscopic preferred over open if available
Single-dose pre-operative antibiotics if uncomplicated
references: JAMA: Appendicitis - Clinical Manifestations and Diagnosis
World Society of Emergency Surgery guidelines for appendicitis

cases.title: Diabetic Patient with Altered Mental Status
cases.presentation: 28-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes presenting with confusion, polyuria, and abdominal pain

history.chief_complaint: My daughter is confused and breathing fast
history.hpi: Patient ran out of insulin 3 days ago. Developed polyuria, polydipsia, nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain. Today became confused and lethargic. Fruity breath odor noted by family.
history.medications: Insulin glargine, insulin lispac (ran out 3 days ago)
history.social: Lives with parents, works retail

physical_exam.abdomen: Diffuse tenderness without guarding
physical_exam.neuro: GCS 13, oriented to person only

cases.explanation: Classic DKA triad: hyperglycemia (>250), metabolic acidosis (pH <7.3, bicarb <18), and ketonemia. Precipitating factor: insulin non-compliance. Clinical features include Kussmaul respirations (respiratory compensation), fruity breath (acetone), dehydration, altered mental status, and abdominal pain (pseudoperitonitis).
management_pearls: ABC stabilization: 2 large-bore IVs, oxygen if needed
Aggressive IV fluids: 1L NS bolus, then 250-500 mL/hr
Insulin infusion: 0.1 units/kg/hr (DO NOT give bolus if K+ <3.3)
Potassium replacement crucial: monitor q2-4h (K+ drops with insulin)
When glucose <250: switch to D5 1/2 NS, continue insulin until anion gap closes
Identify precipitating cause: infection, MI, non-compliance most common
Bicarbonate only if pH <6.9 (controversial)
Transition to subQ insulin when: eating, anion gap normal, pH >7.3
references: ADA: Hyperglycemic Crises in Adults with Diabetes

cases.title: Febrile Child with Stiff Neck
cases.presentation: 18-month-old girl with fever, irritability, and decreased oral intake brought by worried parents

history.chief_complaint: High fever and won't stop crying
history.hpi: Fever to 103°F for 12 hours. Progressive irritability. Vomiting twice. Decreased PO intake. Parents note child cries when picked up. No known sick contacts. Immunizations up to date.
history.social: In daycare

physical_exam.neck: Nuchal rigidity, positive Kernig and Brudzinski signs
physical_exam.skin: Petechial rash on trunk and extremities
physical_exam.neuro: GCS 12, weak cry

labs.lp: Opening pressure 28 cm H2O, WBC 3,500 (90% PMNs), protein 180 mg/dL, glucose 25 mg/dL

imaging.ct_head: No mass effect, LP safe to perform

cases.explanation: Bacterial meningitis: fever, altered mental status, meningismus (nuchal rigidity, Kernig/Brudzinski signs). Petechial rash suggests Neisseria meningitidis. CSF shows: elevated WBC with PMN predominance, elevated protein, low glucose. Classic CSF formula: 'High cells, high protein, low glucose' = bacterial. This is a medical emergency requiring immediate antibiotics.
management_pearls: Do NOT delay antibiotics for LP if unstable or coagulopathy
Empiric antibiotics STAT: Vancomycin + Ceftriaxone (add ampicillin if <1 month or >50 years for Listeria)
Dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg before/with first antibiotic dose (reduces mortality)
Aggressive IV fluids and supportive care
Droplet precautions until bacterial meningitis ruled out
Prophylaxis for close contacts if N. meningitidis confirmed (rifampin or cipro)
Monitor for complications: increased ICP, seizures, SIADH, septic shock
references: IDSA Practice Guidelines for Bacterial Meningitis
Pediatric Bacterial Meningitis: Recognition and Management

cases.title: Man with Sudden Severe Back Pain
cases.presentation: 68-year-old man with sudden-onset severe abdominal and back pain, feeling lightheaded

history.chief_complaint: My back is killing me
history.hpi: Sudden onset severe abdominal pain radiating to back 1 hour ago while lifting groceries. Describes tearing sensation. Feels dizzy. Wife notes he looks pale and sweaty.
history.pmh: Hypertension, hyperlipidemia, known 5cm AAA on surveillance
history.social: Former smoker (quit 10 years ago), 50 pack-year history

physical_exam.abdomen: Tender, pulsatile mass, guarding, no bowel sounds

imaging.bedside_us: Large AAA with hypoechoic rim, free fluid in abdomen

cases.explanation: Ruptured AAA: classic triad of abdominal/back pain, hypotension, and pulsatile abdominal mass. Risk factors present: known AAA, age >65, male, smoking history, HTN. Grey-Turner sign (flank ecchymosis) indicates retroperitoneal hemorrhage. This is immediately life-threatening. Do NOT delay for CT if unstable - go directly to OR!
management_pearls: CALL VASCULAR SURGERY IMMEDIATELY - this is a surgical emergency
Permissive hypotension: Target SBP 80-100 (avoid overresuscitation causing more bleeding)
Massive transfusion protocol: 1:1:1 PRBC:FFP:platelets
2 large-bore IVs, type and cross 10 units PRBC
Do NOT delay for CT if hemodynamically unstable - STAT to OR
Endovascular repair (EVAR) preferred if anatomy suitable and available
Mortality 50% even with surgery - counsel family
Post-op complications: renal failure, bowel ischemia, compartment syndrome
references: SVS Practice Guidelines for Ruptured AAA
Emergency Management of Ruptured Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm

cases.title: Woman with Painful Swollen Leg
cases.presentation: 45-year-old woman with 2 days of left leg pain and swelling after long flight from Europe

history.chief_complaint: My left leg is swollen and hurts
history.hpi: Returned from 10-hour flight 3 days ago. Left calf started hurting 2 days ago. Progressive swelling. Pain worse with walking. No trauma. No chest pain or shortness of breath.
history.social: Works office job, sedentary

physical_exam.extremities: Left calf swollen, 3cm larger than right, tender to palpation, warm, positive Homan's sign

imaging.doppler_ultrasound: Non-compressible left popliteal and femoral veins, intraluminal echogenic material consistent with thrombus

cases.explanation: Provoked DVT with multiple risk factors: recent prolonged travel (>8 hours), OCPs, obesity, sedentary lifestyle, family history. Wells score: leg swelling (1), calf tenderness (1), entire leg swollen (1), recently bedridden/surgery (1.5) = 4.5 points = DVT likely. Ultrasound confirms non-compressible vein with thrombus.
management_pearls: Anticoagulation immediately: Apixaban 10mg BID x 7 days, then 5mg BID OR Rivaroxaban 15mg BID x 21 days, then 20mg daily
Alternative: Enoxaparin 1mg/kg BID bridge to warfarin (if DOACs contraindicated)
Discontinue estrogen-containing contraceptives (thrombogenic)
Compression stockings for symptom relief (not proven to prevent post-thrombotic syndrome)
Encourage early mobilization (bedrest not recommended)
Screen for PE: ask about chest pain, dyspnea, hemoptysis
Duration: Minimum 3 months, consider extended if unprovoked
Repeat ultrasound at 1 week if symptoms worsen (rule out extension)
references: Diagnosis and Management of Acute Deep Vein Thrombosis

cases.title: Elderly Woman Feeling Weak and Tired
cases.presentation: 62-year-old woman with several months of fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance, and constipation

history.chief_complaint: I'm always tired and cold
history.hpi: Progressive fatigue over 6 months. Gained 15 lbs without dietary changes. Feels cold even in warm rooms. Constipation worsening. Dry skin. Hair thinning. Depressed mood.
history.social: Retired teacher

physical_exam.neuro: Delayed deep tendon reflexes (slow relaxation phase)

imaging.thyroid_us: Heterogeneous echotexture consistent with chronic thyroiditis

cases.explanation: Primary hypothyroidism (likely Hashimoto's thyroiditis based on positive anti-TPO antibodies). Classic symptoms: fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance, constipation, dry skin, hair loss, bradycardia, delayed reflexes. Labs show elevated TSH with low free T4. Hypercholesterolemia is common secondary finding.
management_pearls: Levothyroxine: Start 1.6 mcg/kg/day (round to 50, 75, 88, 100 mcg tablets)
Take on empty stomach, 30-60 minutes before breakfast
Recheck TSH in 6-8 weeks, adjust dose by 12.5-25 mcg increments
Goal TSH: 0.5-2.5 mIU/L (lower end for young patients)
Elderly/cardiac disease: Start low (25 mcg), go slow (risk of precipitating MI)
Drug interactions: Iron, calcium, PPIs decrease absorption (separate by 4 hours)
Monitor symptoms and TSH every 6-12 months once stable
Lifelong therapy required in most cases

cases.title: Man with Sudden Vision Loss
cases.presentation: 65-year-old man with sudden, painless loss of vision in right eye 1 hour ago

history.chief_complaint: I can't see out of my right eye
history.hpi: Sudden onset complete vision loss in right eye while reading newspaper. Painless. No preceding symptoms. No trauma. No flashing lights or floaters. Left eye vision normal.
history.social: Smoker 1 PPD x 40 years

physical_exam.eye_exam: Right eye: Light perception only, RAPD present, fundoscopy shows pale retina with cherry red spot at macula
physical_exam.neuro: Otherwise intact, no focal deficits

cases.explanation: Central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO): sudden, painless, complete vision loss. Classic fundoscopic finding is cherry red spot (fovea has dual blood supply, stands out against pale ischemic retina). This is an ocular stroke - 'time is retina'. RAPD confirms afferent pupillary defect. Risk factors: AFib (embolic), carotid stenosis, smoking, HTN. ESR not markedly elevated, making GCA less likely.
management_pearls: THIS IS AN EMERGENCY - Permanent vision loss occurs after 90-100 minutes
Immediate ophthalmology consult
Ocular massage: Firm pressure on eye for 5 sec, release 5 sec, repeat x 5 cycles
Anterior chamber paracentesis (by ophthalmology) to lower IOP
Hyperbaric oxygen if available and <24 hours from onset
ASA 325mg (prevent recurrence)
Start anticoagulation for AFib (warfarin or DOAC)
Workup embolic source: Echo, carotid ultrasound
Consider CEA if severe carotid stenosis (>70%)
Visual recovery poor even with treatment (15-30%)
references: AAO Acute Retinal Artery Occlusion Guidelines
Central Retinal Artery Occlusion: Diagnosis and Management

cases.title: Hypotensive Patient with Fever and Altered Mental Status
cases.presentation: 58-year-old man brought by ambulance with fever, confusion, and low blood pressure

history.chief_complaint: Found confused at home with fever
history.hpi: Family found patient confused this morning. Had urinary symptoms (dysuria, frequency) for 3 days but didn't seek care. Now febrile, lethargic, and incontinent of urine.
history.social: Lives alone, retired

physical_exam.general: Lethargic, responds to painful stimuli only
physical_exam.skin: Mottled, cool extremities, delayed cap refill >4 seconds
physical_exam.abdomen: Suprapubic tenderness
physical_exam.neuro: GCS 10 (E3V2M5)

cases.explanation: Septic shock from urosepsis: SIRS criteria met (temp >38°C, HR >90, RR >20, WBC >12k with bandemia). Hypotension refractory to fluids + elevated lactate = septic shock. Source is urinary (UA findings, suprapubic tenderness). Organ dysfunction: AKI (Cr elevated), altered mental status, hypoxia. qSOFA score 3 (AMS, RR ≥22, SBP ≤100) predicts high mortality.
management_pearls: HOUR-1 BUNDLE (start immediately):
1. Measure lactate (remeasure if >2)
2. Obtain blood cultures BEFORE antibiotics
3. Broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour: Pip-tazo or cefepime + vancomycin
4. 30 mL/kg crystalloid bolus for hypotension/lactate ≥4
5. Vasopressors if hypotensive during/after fluid resuscitation (target MAP ≥65)
Norepinephrine is first-line vasopressor
Source control: Foley catheter (relieve obstruction), consider urology consult
Monitor: Central line, arterial line, continuous vitals
ICU admission for close monitoring
Steroid (hydrocortisone 200mg/day) if vasopressor-dependent
references: Recognition and Management of Septic Shock

cases.title: Man with Sudden Right-Sided Weakness
cases.presentation: 67-year-old man with sudden onset right-sided weakness and slurred speech 90 minutes ago

history.chief_complaint: Right side not working, can't talk right
history.hpi: Wife reports patient was fine at breakfast. Suddenly developed right arm/leg weakness and difficulty speaking at 8:00 AM. Last known normal time 7:30 AM (90 min ago). No seizure, no head trauma. EMS activated stroke alert.
history.social: No smoking, occasional alcohol

physical_exam.neuro: NIHSS 15 - right hemiparesis (arm 3/5, leg 4/5), right facial droop, expressive aphasia, right visual field cut, gaze deviation to left

imaging.ct_head: No hemorrhage, early loss of grey-white differentiation in left MCA territory
imaging.cta_head_neck: Left MCA M1 segment occlusion, no carotid stenosis

cases.explanation: Acute ischemic stroke in left MCA distribution: sudden onset focal neurological deficit (right hemiparesis, aphasia, gaze deviation). NIHSS 15 = moderate-severe. Risk factors: AFib (cardioembolic source), HTN. Within therapeutic window for both tPA (IV thrombolysis) and mechanical thrombectomy. Large vessel occlusion on CTA makes this thrombectomy candidate.
management_pearls: TIME IS BRAIN - Door-to-needle goal <60 minutes
tPA eligibility: <4.5 hours from symptom onset, no hemorrhage on CT, no contraindications
Alteplase 0.9 mg/kg (max 90mg): 10% bolus, 90% over 1 hour
BP management: Keep <185/110 before tPA, <180/105 after tPA
Mechanical thrombectomy: Large vessel occlusion + <6 hours (up to 24h with favorable imaging)
Stat neurology and neurointerventional consult
NPO, aspirin held x 24h post-tPA
Start anticoagulation for AFib after 24h (prevent recurrence)
Stroke unit admission for neuro checks q1-2h
Rehab evaluation early

cases.title: Man with Severe Epigastric Pain After Drinking
cases.presentation: 42-year-old man with severe upper abdominal pain radiating to back after binge drinking

history.chief_complaint: Worst stomach pain of my life
history.hpi: Severe epigastric pain started 6 hours ago after drinking heavily at party. Pain constant, boring, radiates to back. Multiple episodes of vomiting. Pain worse lying flat, better leaning forward. No relief with antacids.
history.pmh: Alcohol use disorder, prior episode of pancreatitis 2 years ago
history.social: Alcohol 8-12 beers daily, smoking 1 PPD

physical_exam.abdomen: Epigastric tenderness without rebound, hypoactive bowel sounds, no Murphy's sign
physical_exam.other: No jaundice, no Grey-Turner or Cullen signs

imaging.ct_abdomen: Pancreatic edema and peripancreatic fat stranding, no necrosis or pseudocyst

cases.explanation: Acute pancreatitis diagnosis requires 2 of 3: (1) Characteristic pain ✓, (2) Lipase >3x ULN ✓, (3) Imaging findings ✓. Etiology is alcohol (GET SMASHED mnemonic). Pain radiating to back, worse supine, better leaning forward is classic. Hypocalcemia suggests more severe disease. No signs of necrotizing pancreatitis (no Grey-Turner/Cullen signs).
management_pearls: Aggressive IV fluid resuscitation: Lactated Ringer's 250-500 mL/hr (decreases mortality)
Goal: UOP >0.5 mL/kg/hr, Hct stable, BUN decreasing
Pain control: IV opioids (morphine, hydromorphone)
NPO initially, advance diet when pain improves (no need to wait for lipase normalization)
Ranson criteria at admission and 48h (predicts mortality)
ERCP only if gallstone pancreatitis with cholangitis/obstruction
No routine antibiotics (unless infected necrosis)
Monitor for complications: necrosis, pseudocyst, abscess, ARDS, AKI
Alcohol cessation counseling and addiction treatment referral
references: ACG Guidelines for Management of Acute Pancreatitis
cases.author: Dr. Gastroenterology

cases.title: Woman with Decreased Urine Output
cases.presentation: 68-year-old woman with 2 days of decreased urine output, nausea, and confusion

history.chief_complaint: Not peeing much, feeling sick
history.hpi: Started new BP medication (lisinopril) 1 week ago. Developed diarrhea 3 days ago (viral gastroenteritis). Urine output markedly decreased past 2 days. Nausea, vomiting. Daughter notes confusion.
history.social: Lives with daughter

physical_exam.abdomen: Soft, no masses

labs.urinalysis: Specific gravity 1.030, no protein, no blood, no casts

cases.explanation: Acute kidney injury (Cr increased 2.4x from baseline) with prerenal etiology. Risk factors: volume depletion (diarrhea, poor PO intake), ACE inhibitor (decreases GFR), NSAIDs (decrease renal perfusion), CKD. Physical exam shows hypovolemia (orthostasis, dry mucous membranes, tachycardia). Labs support prerenal: BUN:Cr ratio >20:1, FENa <1%, urine Na <20, concentrated urine (high specific gravity). No hydronephrosis rules out postrenal.
management_pearls: STOP nephrotoxins: ACE inhibitor, NSAIDs, any other offending drugs
IV fluid resuscitation: Normal saline 500-1000 mL bolus, then maintenance
Monitor UOP, daily weights, strict I/Os
Trend Cr daily (should improve with fluids if prerenal)
Hyperkalemia management if K >6.0 or EKG changes: Calcium gluconate, insulin/dextrose, kayexalate
Avoid contrast, aminoglycosides, other nephrotoxins
Adjust medication doses for renal function
Urology consult only if hydronephrosis (postrenal)
Nephrology consult if: No improvement with fluids, intrinsic AKI, need dialysis (K >6.5, pH <7.1, volume overload, uremia)
references: Acute Kidney Injury: Diagnosis and Management
cases.author: Dr. Nephrology

cases.title: Woman with Sudden Difficulty Breathing After Bee Sting
cases.presentation: 32-year-old woman with sudden onset shortness of breath, throat tightness, and rash 5 minutes after bee sting

history.chief_complaint: Can't breathe, throat closing up
history.hpi: Stung by bee in garden 5 minutes ago. Immediately developed itching, then hives over whole body. Now complains throat feels tight, hard to swallow, difficulty breathing. Dizzy and nauseated. No prior bee sting reactions.
history.social: Teacher, married

physical_exam.abdomen: Cramping

cases.explanation: Classic anaphylaxis: rapid onset (<minutes) of allergic symptoms involving ≥2 organ systems after allergen exposure (bee sting). Criteria met: (1) Skin involvement (urticaria, angioedema) + (2) Respiratory compromise (wheezing, stridor) + (3) Cardiovascular compromise (hypotension, tachycardia). Life-threatening emergency requiring immediate epinephrine.
management_pearls: EPINEPHRINE FIRST: 0.3-0.5 mg IM (1:1000) in anterolateral thigh - DO NOT DELAY
Can repeat q5-15 min if no improvement
Call for help/activate emergency response
Position supine with legs elevated (or left lateral if pregnant/vomiting)
High-flow oxygen via non-rebreather
IV access: 1-2L NS bolus for hypotension
Adjunct therapy (NOT substitutes for epi): H1-blocker (diphenhydramine 50mg IV), H2-blocker (ranitidine 50mg IV), steroid (methylprednisolone 125mg IV), albuterol nebulizer
Monitor 4-6 hours minimum (biphasic reaction occurs in 20%)
Discharge with EpiPen x2 and education on use
Allergy/immunology referral for venom immunotherapy

cases.title: COPD Patient with Worsening Shortness of Breath
cases.presentation: 65-year-old man with known COPD presenting with 3 days of increased dyspnea, cough, and purulent sputum

history.chief_complaint: Can't catch my breath
history.hpi: COPD on home O2 (2L NC baseline). Developed URI symptoms 5 days ago. Progressive dyspnea, increased cough with yellow-green sputum, chest tightness. Using rescue inhaler every 2 hours without relief. No fever.
history.social: 60 pack-year smoking history (quit 2 years ago)

physical_exam.vitals: BP 145/85, HR 102, RR 28, O2 85% on 2L NC, Temp 98.6°F
physical_exam.general: Tripod position, using accessory muscles, speaking in short sentences
physical_exam.lungs: Diffuse expiratory wheezing, prolonged expiratory phase, decreased breath sounds
physical_exam.neuro: Alert, no asterixis

labs.abg: pH 7.32, pCO2 58, pO2 55, HCO3 30 (acute on chronic respiratory acidosis)

imaging.cxr: Hyperinflation, flattened diaphragms, no consolidation or pneumothorax

cases.explanation: COPD exacerbation defined by acute worsening of respiratory symptoms beyond normal variation. Anthonisen criteria present: (1) Increased dyspnea ✓, (2) Increased sputum volume ✓, (3) Sputum purulence ✓ = Type 1 (most severe). ABG shows acute on chronic hypercapnic respiratory failure. No evidence of pneumonia (afebrile, no consolidation on CXR). Triggered by viral URI.
management_pearls: Oxygen: Titrate to SpO2 88-92% (avoid CO2 retention from over-oxygenation)
Bronchodilators: Albuterol/ipratropium nebs q4h or continuous
Systemic steroids: Prednisone 40mg PO daily x 5 days (decreases recovery time, prevents relapse)
Antibiotics if purulent sputum: Azithromycin or doxycycline x 5 days
Consider BiPAP if: pH <7.35, pCO2 >45, RR >25, accessory muscle use
Intubation criteria: pH <7.25, declining mental status, BiPAP failure
Avoid sedatives (worsen hypoventilation)
Smoking cessation counseling
Pulmonary rehab referral
Ensure proper inhaler technique and adherence
cases.author: Dr. Pulmonary Medicine

cases.title: Man Vomiting Blood
cases.presentation: 52-year-old man with history of alcohol abuse presenting with hematemesis and melena

history.chief_complaint: Throwing up blood
history.hpi: Two episodes of vomiting large amounts of bright red blood in past hour. Reports black, tarry stools x 2 days. Feeling dizzy and weak. Drinks heavily, history of chronic liver disease. No NSAIDs or anticoagulants.
history.pmh: Cirrhosis (alcohol-related), known esophageal varices, no prior bleeds
history.social: Alcohol abuse, vodka 1 pint daily

physical_exam.abdomen: Distended, fluid wave, mild tenderness, liver edge palpable, splenomegaly
physical_exam.neuro: Alert but confused, asterixis present

cases.explanation: Variceal upper GI bleed in cirrhotic patient: hematemesis (bright red blood = active bleeding), melena, hemodynamic instability. Glasgow-Blatchford score high (predicts need for intervention). Risk factors: known varices, stopped beta-blocker prophylaxis. Signs of chronic liver disease: ascites, jaundice, coagulopathy, thrombocytopenia, spider angiomas. BUN:Cr ratio >30 suggests upper GI source. This is life-threatening emergency.
management_pearls: ABC resuscitation: 2 large-bore IVs (16-18G), aggressive crystalloid
Blood products: Transfuse PRBC goal Hgb 7-9 (over-transfusion increases portal pressure), FFP if INR >2.5, platelets if <50k
Octreotide 50 mcg bolus, then 50 mcg/hr infusion (decreases splanchnic blood flow)
Antibiotics: Ceftriaxone 1g IV (reduces mortality, prevents SBP)
PPI: Pantoprazole 80mg bolus, then 8mg/hr infusion
URGENT EGD within 12 hours (preferably <6h if unstable)
Band ligation preferred over sclerotherapy for varices
If refractory: Sengstaken-Blakemore tube (temporizing), TIPS
Secondary prophylaxis: Non-selective beta-blocker (propranolol or carvedilol) + repeat EGD for surveillance
references: ACG Guidelines for Management of Variceal Hemorrhage
Upper GI Bleeding: Management and Outcomes
cases.author: Dr. Gastroenterology

cases.title: Elderly Woman with Shortness of Breath and Leg Swelling
cases.presentation: 78-year-old woman with progressive shortness of breath, orthopnea, and bilateral leg swelling over 1 week

history.chief_complaint: Can't breathe when I lie down
history.hpi: Progressive dyspnea over 1 week. Now can only sleep propped up on 3 pillows (orthopnea). Wakes up gasping for air at night (PND). Bilateral leg swelling. 10 lb weight gain. Cough with pink frothy sputum. Ran out of 'water pill' 2 weeks ago.
history.pmh: CHF with reduced EF 30%, CAD s/p MI, hypertension, diabetes
history.medications: Lisinopril, metoprolol, atorvastatin, furosemide (stopped 2 weeks ago)
history.social: Lives alone, diet non-compliant (ate salty foods)

physical_exam.abdomen: Soft, hepatomegaly

imaging.cxr: Cardiomegaly, bilateral pleural effusions, Kerley B lines, cephalization

cases.explanation: Acute decompensated heart failure (ADHF): Framingham criteria met with multiple major criteria (PND, orthopnea, JVP elevated, S3 gallop, pulmonary edema on CXR) and minor criteria (edema, hepatomegaly). Precipitating factors: medication non-compliance (stopped furosemide), dietary indiscretion (high salt intake). BNP >500 confirms CHF. Wet and warm hemodynamic profile (volume overload without hypoperfusion).
management_pearls: Oxygen: Non-rebreather or BiPAP if severe respiratory distress
IV diuretics: Furosemide 40-80mg IV bolus (2.5x home dose if on chronic furosemide)
Goal: Net negative 1-2L daily, monitor strict I/Os, daily weights
ACE inhibitor: Continue home dose if normotensive (already on lisinopril)
Nitroglycerin: If HTN or flash pulmonary edema (reduces preload/afterload)
Avoid IV fluids (worsens volume overload)
Morphine controversial (may increase mortality)
Telemetry monitoring, troponin to rule out ACS
Once euvolemic: Restart GDMT (ACE-I, beta-blocker, aldosterone antagonist)
Discharge planning: Low-sodium diet (<2g/day), daily weights, medication adherence, cardiology follow-up

cases.title: Young Man with Convulsions
cases.presentation: 24-year-old man brought by EMS actively seizing for 10 minutes, no improvement with 2 doses midazolam

cases.explanation: Status epilepticus: continuous seizure >5 minutes or recurrent seizures without return to baseline. This is medical emergency with high mortality if not controlled rapidly. Cause: antiepileptic medication non-compliance (phenytoin level undetectable). Failed prehospital benzodiazepines = established status epilepticus requiring escalation. Complications: hypoxia, hyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis, cerebral edema.
management_pearls: TIME-BASED PROTOCOL:
0-5 min: ABC stabilization, check glucose (if low give D50), benzodiazepine
Lorazepam 4mg IV (or diazepam 10mg IV, or midazolam 10mg IM if no IV)
Can repeat once after 5 min if continues
5-20 min (established SE): Second-line AED
Fosphenytoin 20 PE/kg IV at max 150 PE/min OR
Levetiracetam 60 mg/kg IV (max 4500mg) OR
Valproic acid 40 mg/kg IV
20-40 min (refractory SE): Continuous infusion + intubation
Propofol, midazolam, or pentobarbital drip
EEG monitoring for burst suppression
ICU admission for refractory cases
Identify and treat underlying cause
references: Neurocritical Care Society Status Epilepticus Guidelines

cases.explanation: Septic arthritis: acute monoarticular arthritis with fever. Synovial fluid WBC >50,000 with PMN predominance strongly suggests bacterial infection. Gram stain positive for Staph aureus (most common organism). Risk factors: recent intra-articular injection, diabetes. This is orthopedic emergency - untreated leads to joint destruction. Cannot be gout (no crystals, WBC typically lower in gout).

Arthrocentesis: Drain joint completely, send for cell count, Gram stain, culture
Empiric IV antibiotics immediately after cultures: Vancomycin + ceftriaxone (covers MRSA and GNRs)
Switch to organism-specific therapy when culture results available
Surgical drainage: Arthroscopic washout preferred (open if hip/shoulder)
Daily aspirations if not surgical candidate
IV antibiotics minimum 2 weeks, then PO to complete 4-6 weeks total
Monitor inflammatory markers (ESR, CRP) - should downtrend
Physical therapy once infection controlled
Complications if untreated: cartilage destruction, osteomyelitis, sepsis

Acute Septic Arthritis: Diagnosis and Treatment

history.chief_complaint: Sudden chest pain and difficulty breathing for 2 hours

history.social: Non-smoker, college student

labs.abg: pH 7.48, pCO2 32, pO2 75 (mild hypoxemia, respiratory alkalosis)

imaging.cxr: Right-sided pneumothorax, approximately 30% lung collapse, no mediastinal shift

cases.explanation: Primary spontaneous pneumothorax typically affects tall, thin young adults (especially males, but females on OCPs have increased risk). Key features: (1) Sudden pleuritic chest pain, (2) Dyspnea, (3) Decreased breath sounds and hyperresonance on affected side, (4) CXR showing visceral pleural line separated from chest wall, (5) Absence of underlying lung disease. Family history is common. OCPs increase risk in women.
management_pearls: Small pneumothorax (<2cm, <20%): Observation and supplemental O2 (accelerates reabsorption)
Large pneumothorax (>2cm or symptomatic): Chest tube placement (pigtail catheter or traditional)
Tension pneumothorax (clinical diagnosis): Immediate needle decompression 2nd ICS midclavicular line
Recurrence prevention: Consider VATS with pleurodesis for recurrent pneumothorax
Discharge counseling: Avoid flying/diving until resolved, seek immediate care for recurrent symptoms
pitfalls: Don't wait for CXR if tension pneumothorax suspected (hemodynamic instability, tracheal deviation)
Small pneumothorax can be missed on standard PA CXR - consider expiratory or lateral decubitus films
Young women on OCPs have higher risk - consider in differential for chest pain/dyspnea

cases.title: Confusion and Fever in Nursing Home Resident

history.chief_complaint: Confusion and not eating
history.hpi: Nursing home resident with baseline dementia. Staff report patient has been 'not herself' for 2 days - more confused than usual, refusing meals, and had one episode of urinary incontinence (unusual for her). No reported cough, chest pain, or dysuria.

history.social: Nursing home resident, non-smoker

physical_exam.abdomen: Soft, mild suprapubic tenderness
physical_exam.neuro: Alert to voice but confused, no focal deficits

labs.urinalysis: WBC >100, nitrite positive, bacteria present, 5-10 RBC

cases.explanation: UTI is a common cause of delirium in elderly patients. Classic UTI symptoms (dysuria, frequency) are often absent in geriatric patients. Key features: (1) Acute change in mental status from baseline, (2) Low-grade fever, (3) Suprapubic tenderness, (4) Pyuria with positive nitrites and culture, (5) Elevated WBC with left shift. The confusion is often the primary manifestation. Acute kidney injury suggests complicated UTI.
management_pearls: Start empiric antibiotics after cultures obtained - consider local resistance patterns
Ceftriaxone 1g IV daily or fluoroquinolone if local resistance <10%
Adjust antibiotics based on culture and sensitivities
Hydration and close monitoring for sepsis progression
Treat 7-14 days for complicated UTI (AKI, altered mental status)
Address prevention: adequate hydration, regular toileting, avoid unnecessary catheters
pitfalls: Asymptomatic bacteriuria is common in nursing homes - don't treat UA alone without symptoms
Confusion may be sole presenting symptom of serious infection in elderly
Consider alternative sources: pneumonia, C. diff, medication effects
Prolonged confusion after treatment is common - may take days to return to baseline

cases.title: Young Man with Severe Headache and Stiff Neck

Understand timing of antibiotics vs. lumbar puncture
Apply CSF analysis for differential diagnosis
cases.presentation: 19-year-old college student with severe headache, fever, and neck stiffness for 6 hours

history.chief_complaint: Worst headache of my life and can't bend my neck
history.hpi: Patient developed sudden severe headache this morning, worse than any previous headache. Associated with fever, photophobia, nausea with vomiting. Roommate reports patient seems confused. No recent trauma. One episode of similar but milder symptoms 2 weeks ago that resolved.
history.pmh: No significant medical history, up to date on vaccinations except missed MenACWY booster
history.social: College freshman living in dormitory, non-smoker, occasional alcohol

physical_exam.heent: Pupils equal and reactive, no papilledema
physical_exam.neck: Marked nuchal rigidity, positive Kernig and Brudzinski signs
physical_exam.skin: Petechial rash on trunk and lower extremities
physical_exam.neuro: Alert but confused, GCS 14, no focal deficits

labs.csf: Opening pressure 350 mmH2O, WBC 2,800 (95% PMNs), glucose 15, protein 220, Gram stain shows Gram-negative diplococci

imaging.ct_head: No mass effect, midline shift, or hemorrhage

cases.explanation: Bacterial meningitis is a medical emergency. Classic triad (fever, headache, neck stiffness) present in only 44% but nearly all have 2/3 symptoms. Key features: (1) Acute onset severe headache with fever, (2) Meningismus with positive Kernig/Brudzinski signs, (3) Altered mental status, (4) Petechial rash (suggests N. meningitidis), (5) CSF with high WBC (PMN predominant), low glucose, high protein, (6) Gram stain showing organisms. College dormitory living is risk factor for meningococcal meningitis.
management_pearls: DO NOT DELAY ANTIBIOTICS for LP - give within 1 hour of presentation if bacterial meningitis suspected
Empiric antibiotics: Vancomycin + Ceftriaxone (add ampicillin if >50yo or immunocompromised for Listeria coverage)
Dexamethasone 10mg IV before or with first antibiotic dose (reduces mortality in pneumococcal meningitis)
LP can be done after antibiotics started - CSF culture may be positive for up to 48 hours
Droplet precautions until bacterial meningitis ruled out or 24h of antibiotics
Chemoprophylaxis for close contacts if N. meningitidis confirmed (rifampin, ciprofloxacin, or ceftriaxone)
pitfalls: CT head before LP only if: focal neuro deficit, papilledema, immunocompromised, or altered consciousness - don't delay antibiotics
Classic triad present in <50% of cases - maintain high suspicion with fever + headache or AMS + fever
Petechial rash with fever and headache = meningococcemia until proven otherwise - this is rapidly fatal
Viral vs bacterial: CSF lymphocytic predominance, normal/high glucose suggests viral; PMN predominance, low glucose suggests bacterial

cases.title: Postpartum Woman with Painful, Swollen Leg
learning_objectives: Recognize risk factors for postpartum DVT
cases.presentation: 28-year-old woman 2 weeks postpartum with left leg swelling and pain

history.chief_complaint: Left leg swelling and pain for 3 days
history.hpi: Patient delivered via emergency C-section 2 weeks ago. Developed left calf pain 3 days ago, initially thought it was muscle strain. Pain worsened and leg became swollen. Denies chest pain or shortness of breath. No fever. Currently breastfeeding.
history.pmh: No significant medical history prior to pregnancy
history.ob_history: G2P2, emergency C-section for fetal distress after prolonged labor (18 hours), estimated blood loss 800 mL
history.social: Non-smoker, no alcohol, married

physical_exam.extremities: Left leg: 3cm greater circumference than right at calf, tender over deep venous system, positive Homan's sign, no erythema or warmth, palpable cord

imaging.leg_ultrasound: Non-compressible left common femoral and popliteal veins consistent with acute DVT, clot extends to calf veins

cases.explanation: Pregnancy and postpartum period are hypercoagulable states with 5-10x increased DVT risk. Risk peaks at 3-6 weeks postpartum. Key features: (1) Postpartum state (especially post-C-section), (2) Unilateral leg swelling and pain, (3) >3cm leg circumference difference, (4) Positive Homan's sign (low sensitivity but specific), (5) Compression ultrasound showing non-compressible vein, (6) Additional risk factors: emergency C-section, prolonged labor, blood loss, family history. D-dimer unreliable in pregnancy/postpartum due to physiologic elevation.
management_pearls: Anticoagulation safe in breastfeeding: LMWH (enoxaparin) preferred, warfarin acceptable, DOACs not recommended
Start enoxaparin 1mg/kg SC twice daily immediately (don't wait for imaging if high suspicion)
Continue anticoagulation for minimum 3-6 months postpartum
Monitor for PE symptoms - lower threshold for CTPE if any respiratory symptoms
Compression stockings for symptom relief (30-40 mmHg)
Can resume full activity as tolerated, encourage ambulation
pitfalls: D-dimer unreliable in pregnancy/postpartum - don't use to rule out DVT
Leg swelling common postpartum - but unilateral swelling >3cm difference is abnormal
Pregnancy-associated VTE has higher risk of recurrence - some need long-term anticoagulation
Screen for thrombophilia if unprovoked or recurrent VTE, strong family history, or young age

Understand importance of early treatment to prevent coronary complications

cases.presentation: 4-year-old boy with 5 days of high fever, rash, red eyes, and swollen hands

history.chief_complaint: High fever for 5 days not responding to ibuprofen
history.hpi: Previously healthy child developed fever 5 days ago (103-104°F), not responding well to antipyretics. Parents also noticed red eyes (no discharge), red cracked lips, red tongue, rash on trunk, and swollen red hands and feet. Child has been irritable and decreased oral intake. No cough, vomiting, or diarrhea.
history.pmh: Healthy, up to date on immunizations
history.social: Attends preschool, no sick contacts, no recent travel

physical_exam.heent: Bilateral non-exudative conjunctival injection, dry cracked erythematous lips, strawberry tongue, pharyngeal erythema without exudate, no cervical lymphadenopathy >1.5cm
physical_exam.skin: Polymorphous erythematous rash on trunk, peeling of fingers and toes starting, erythema and edema of hands and feet
physical_exam.extremities: Warm, swollen, tender hands and feet

imaging.echocardiogram: Normal coronary arteries, no aneurysms, mild mitral regurgitation

cases.explanation: Kawasaki disease is an acute febrile vasculitis affecting medium-sized arteries, especially coronary arteries. Diagnosis requires fever ≥5 days PLUS ≥4 of 5 criteria: (1) Bilateral non-exudative conjunctivitis ✓, (2) Oral changes (cracked lips, strawberry tongue, pharyngeal erythema) ✓, (3) Polymorphous rash ✓, (4) Extremity changes (erythema/edema in acute phase, periungual desquamation later) ✓, (5) Cervical lymphadenopathy >1.5cm (✗ absent). This patient has 4/5 criteria with supportive labs (thrombocytosis, elevated ESR/CRP, low albumin). Treatment must be initiated within 10 days to prevent coronary artery aneurysms.
management_pearls: IVIG 2 g/kg as single infusion - give within 10 days of fever onset (ideally within 7 days)
High-dose aspirin 80-100 mg/kg/day divided QID until fever resolves, then low-dose 3-5 mg/kg/day
Baseline echocardiogram and repeat at 2 weeks and 6-8 weeks
If IVIG-resistant (fever >36h after IVIG), consider second IVIG dose or corticosteroids
Avoid live vaccines for 11 months after IVIG due to interference
Long-term cardiology follow-up based on coronary involvement
pitfalls: Incomplete Kawasaki disease (<4 criteria) can still cause coronary aneurysms - use echo and inflammatory markers to guide treatment
Peak age 6 months - 5 years, but can occur at any age including infants and adolescents
Thrombocytosis typically occurs in second week - may see normal or low platelets in acute phase
Treatment delayed beyond 10 days still beneficial but higher risk of coronary complications

cases.title: Young Woman with Palpitations and Weight Loss
learning_objectives: Differentiate Graves' disease from other causes of thyrotoxicosis
cases.presentation: 26-year-old woman with palpitations, anxiety, heat intolerance, and 15-pound weight loss over 2 months

history.chief_complaint: Racing heart and can't stop losing weight
history.hpi: Patient reports 2 months of progressive symptoms: heart racing even at rest, feeling anxious and jittery, can't tolerate heat, excessive sweating, difficulty sleeping. Lost 15 pounds despite increased appetite. Also reports frequent loose stools, hand tremor, and feeling like eyes are 'bulging out'. Menstrual periods have been irregular.
history.social: Graphic designer, non-smoker, occasional alcohol, high stress job
history.family: Mother has hypothyroidism, maternal aunt has Graves' disease

physical_exam.general: Anxious-appearing, restless, warm and diaphoretic skin
physical_exam.heent: Lid lag, exophthalmos, infrequent blinking, diffusely enlarged thyroid (3x normal size), no nodules, bruit over thyroid
physical_exam.neuro: Fine tremor of outstretched hands, hyperreflexia

imaging.thyroid_ultrasound: Diffusely enlarged, heterogeneous, hypervascular gland consistent with Graves' disease
imaging.radioiodine_uptake: 45% at 24 hours (markedly elevated, normal 10-30%) with diffuse uptake

cases.explanation: Graves' disease is the most common cause of hyperthyroidism, caused by TSH-receptor antibodies (TSI). Key features: (1) Hyperthyroid symptoms: weight loss, palpitations, heat intolerance, anxiety, tremor, (2) Diffusely enlarged thyroid with bruit, (3) Graves' ophthalmopathy: exophthalmos, lid lag, (4) Suppressed TSH with elevated free T4/T3, (5) Positive TSI antibodies, (6) Diffusely increased radioiodine uptake. Family history of autoimmune thyroid disease is common. More common in women aged 20-40.
management_pearls: Initial treatment options: (1) Antithyroid drugs (methimazole preferred over PTU except in pregnancy), (2) Radioactive iodine ablation, (3) Thyroidectomy
Start methimazole 10-30 mg daily (higher doses for severe hyperthyroidism)
Beta-blocker for symptom control: propranolol 20-40 mg TID-QID or atenolol 25-100 mg daily
Monitor thyroid function every 4-6 weeks initially, adjust medications to achieve euthyroid state
Ophthalmology referral for thyroid eye disease - may need steroids or orbital decompression
Counsel on smoking cessation - worsens eye disease
pitfalls: Check CBC before starting methimazole - rare but serious risk of agranulocytosis (0.1-0.5%)
PTU preferred in first trimester pregnancy and thyroid storm due to less placental transfer
Thyroid storm: life-threatening - fever, tachycardia >140, altered mental status, heart failure. Needs ICU care.
Distinguish from subacute thyroiditis (painful gland, low radioiodine uptake) - no antithyroid drugs needed

cases.title: Teenager with Severe Abdominal Pain and Vomiting
learning_objectives: Understand progression and complications of untreated appendicitis
Apply Alvarado score for risk stratification
cases.presentation: 16-year-old boy with progressively worsening right lower quadrant pain, nausea, and vomiting for 24 hours

history.chief_complaint: Stomach pain that started around belly button and moved to right side
history.hpi: Pain began yesterday evening as vague periumbilical discomfort. Over 6-8 hours, pain migrated to right lower quadrant and became sharper and more severe. Any movement worsens pain. Has had several episodes of vomiting. Decreased appetite - hasn't eaten since yesterday. No diarrhea. Low-grade fever at home.
history.social: High school student, plays soccer, non-smoker

physical_exam.general: Lying still, appears uncomfortable, guarding abdomen
physical_exam.abdomen: Decreased bowel sounds, tenderness and guarding in right lower quadrant, positive McBurney's point tenderness, positive Rovsing's sign, positive psoas sign, negative Murphy's sign, rebound tenderness present

imaging.ct_abdomen_pelvis: Dilated, fluid-filled appendix measuring 1.2cm diameter with surrounding fat stranding. Appendicolith present. No evidence of perforation or abscess.

cases.explanation: Acute appendicitis is the most common surgical emergency. Classic presentation: periumbilical pain migrating to RLQ (as visceral pain becomes somatic), anorexia, nausea/vomiting, fever. Key physical findings: RLQ tenderness at McBurney's point (1/3 distance from ASIS to umbilicus), positive Rovsing's sign (RLQ pain with LLQ palpation), positive psoas sign (pain with hip extension), guarding and rebound tenderness. Alvarado score ≥7 suggests high probability. CT shows dilated appendix >6mm with fat stranding. Appendicolith present in 25% - increases perforation risk.
management_pearls: NPO, IV fluids, analgesia (pain control does not mask diagnosis - give adequate analgesia)
Antibiotics: ceftriaxone + metronidazole OR piperacillin-tazobactam
Urgent appendectomy (laparoscopic preferred) - ideally within 12-24 hours
If perforated: interval appendectomy approach may be considered - antibiotics and percutaneous drainage of abscess, appendectomy 6-8 weeks later
Single-dose prophylactic antibiotics if non-perforated, continue 4-7 days if perforated
pitfalls: Atypical presentations common: retrocecal appendix may present with flank pain or irritative urinary symptoms
CT has 95% sensitivity but consider MRI in pregnancy or ultrasound in children to avoid radiation
Don't rely on normal WBC to rule out appendicitis - 10% have normal WBC
Perforated appendicitis may have temporary improvement in pain (pressure relief) followed by peritonitis

cases.title: Chronic Fatigue and Easy Bruising in Middle-Aged Woman

Understand urgency of diagnosis and treatment

history.chief_complaint: Extreme tiredness and bruising easily
history.hpi: Patient reports feeling increasingly tired over past 6 weeks, unable to perform usual activities. Has had low-grade fevers on and off. Noticed multiple bruises on legs without trauma. Gums bleed when brushing teeth. Had two nosebleeds in past week. Some night sweats. Feels full quickly when eating. No significant weight loss but decreased appetite.
history.pmh: No significant medical history, last saw doctor 2 years ago
history.social: Office manager, non-smoker, occasional alcohol, divorced
history.family: Father died of 'blood cancer' in his 50s

physical_exam.heent: Conjunctival pallor, gingival hypertrophy with bleeding, petechiae on oral mucosa
physical_exam.abdomen: Splenomegaly 4cm below costal margin, mild hepatomegaly
physical_exam.skin: Widespread petechiae, multiple ecchymoses on extremities, no rash

labs.peripheral_smear: Numerous myeloblasts with Auer rods present
labs.dic_panel: PT/PTT mildly prolonged, fibrinogen low, D-dimer elevated

cases.explanation: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is a malignancy of myeloid progenitor cells causing bone marrow failure. Key features: (1) Cytopenias: anemia (fatigue, pallor), thrombocytopenia (bruising, bleeding, petechiae), neutropenia (fever), (2) Circulating blasts >20% with Auer rods (pathognomonic for AML), (3) Organomegaly: hepatosplenomegaly, (4) Gingival hypertrophy (especially M4/M5 subtypes), (5) Elevated LDH and uric acid (tumor lysis), (6) DIC (especially M3-APL subtype). Family history suggests possible hereditary predisposition. This is a hematologic emergency requiring immediate treatment.
management_pearls: URGENT hematology consult - same day
Bone marrow biopsy with flow cytometry, cytogenetics, molecular testing for risk stratification
Tumor lysis syndrome prophylaxis: aggressive IV hydration, allopurinol or rasburicase
Transfusion support: platelets if <10,000 or bleeding, PRBCs for symptomatic anemia
Induction chemotherapy: 7+3 regimen (cytarabine x 7 days + anthracycline x 3 days)
If M3-APL suspected (DIC, young age): START ATRA immediately - highly curable subtype
pitfalls: APL (M3) can present with life-threatening DIC - initiate ATRA before confirmatory testing if high suspicion
Don't delay workup for dental procedures - gingival bleeding will improve with platelet transfusions
Leukostasis (WBC >100,000) is an emergency - may need leukapheresis and immediate chemotherapy
Avoid aspirin, NSAIDs, anticoagulants in setting of severe thrombocytopenia

history.hpi: Patient was lifting a heavy beam at work 3 days ago when felt sudden sharp pain in lower back. Pain radiates from lower back down back of right thigh and calf to lateral foot. Describes electric shock-like, burning pain. Pain worse with coughing, sneezing, or bending forward. Tried ibuprofen and rest with minimal relief. Denies bowel/bladder symptoms. No numbness in saddle area. Can still walk but with severe pain.

history.social: Construction worker, smokes half PPD, occasional alcohol

physical_exam.general: Uncomfortable, slow gait, favoring right leg
physical_exam.spine: Paraspinal muscle spasm, tenderness over L5-S1, loss of normal lumbar lordosis
physical_exam.neuro_lower_extremity: Right ankle dorsiflexion 4/5 (weak), EHL 4/5, ankle plantar flexion 5/5, knee extension 5/5. Sensation decreased over lateral right foot and calf. Patellar reflex 2+ bilateral, Achilles reflex absent on right. Positive straight leg raise on right at 30 degrees, negative on left.

labs.not_indicated: Labs not routinely indicated for acute mechanical back pain without red flags

cases.explanation: L5-S1 disc herniation with S1 radiculopathy. Classic presentation: (1) Acute onset with lifting mechanism, (2) Radicular pain following S1 dermatomal distribution (posterior thigh, lateral calf, lateral foot), (3) Neurologic deficits in S1 distribution: weak ankle plantar flexion (though often normal as here), absent Achilles reflex, lateral foot numbness, (4) Positive straight leg raise <60 degrees (high specificity), (5) MRI confirms disc herniation compressing nerve root. No cauda equina red flags: normal rectal tone, no saddle anesthesia, intact bowel/bladder function.
management_pearls: Conservative management first: NSAIDs, activity modification (avoid bed rest - maintain activity as tolerated), physical therapy
Consider short course of oral steroids (prednisone 60mg x 5 days) or epidural steroid injection for severe pain
Muscle relaxants (cyclobenzaprine) for muscle spasm, short-term opioids only if severe pain uncontrolled
~90% improve with conservative management over 6-12 weeks
Refer to spine surgery if: progressive neurologic deficit, severe intractable pain after 6 weeks conservative therapy, or cauda equina syndrome (urgent surgical decompression)
pitfalls: RED FLAGS requiring urgent MRI and neurosurgical consult: saddle anesthesia, bowel/bladder dysfunction (cauda equina), progressive motor weakness, fever/weight loss/cancer history (infection/malignancy)
MRI not needed acutely unless red flags present - most improve with conservative care
Crossed straight leg raise (pain in affected leg when opposite leg raised) is highly specific for disc herniation
L5 radiculopathy: big toe dorsiflexion weakness, top of foot numbness; S1 radiculopathy: ankle weakness, lateral foot numbness

Understand importance of vascular assessment in diabetic foot
Apply principles of diabetic foot ulcer management
cases.presentation: 62-year-old man with diabetes presenting with red, swollen, painful right foot with drainage from ulcer for 1 week

history.chief_complaint: My foot is red and swollen with pus coming out
history.hpi: Patient with long-standing poorly controlled diabetes noticed small blister on bottom of right foot 3 weeks ago. Didn't think much of it. Over past week, area became larger, red, swollen, and started draining yellow pus. Increasing pain. Fever and chills for 2 days. Denies trauma but admits he walks barefoot at home. Cannot feel his feet well for years.

history.medications: Metformin 1000mg BID, glipizide 10mg BID, lisinopril 20mg daily, atorvastatin 40mg daily
history.social: Retired, smokes 1 PPD x 40 years, poor medication adherence

physical_exam.foot_exam: 3cm plantar ulcer on right first metatarsal head, probe-to-bone positive, purulent drainage, surrounding erythema extending to midfoot, foot edematous and warm, foul odor, crepitus on palpation
physical_exam.vascular: Diminished dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses bilaterally, ABI 0.6 on right (PAD), capillary refill >3 seconds

imaging.mri_foot: First metatarsal osteomyelitis with bone marrow edema, extensive soft tissue infection with abscess formation

cases.explanation: Diabetic foot infection with osteomyelitis - limb-threatening emergency. Key features: (1) Diabetic neuropathy: loss of protective sensation → unrecognized trauma → ulceration, (2) Peripheral arterial disease: poor wound healing, (3) Probe-to-bone positive: high specificity for osteomyelitis, (4) Severe infection: erythema >2cm, purulent drainage, crepitus (gas in tissues), fever, elevated WBC/ESR/CRP, (5) Osteomyelitis on imaging: periosteal reaction, bone marrow edema on MRI, (6) Polymicrobial infection common. This is a PEDIS grade 3-4 infection requiring hospitalization.
management_pearls: ADMIT for IV antibiotics, surgical evaluation, vascular assessment
Broad-spectrum IV antibiotics: vancomycin + piperacillin-tazobactam OR carbapenem, tailor to cultures
Urgent vascular surgery consult - ABI 0.6 indicates critical ischemia, may need revascularization before healing possible
Surgical debridement of necrotic tissue, possible partial foot amputation if extensive osteomyelitis/gangrene
Osteomyelitis treatment: 6+ weeks IV antibiotics (based on bone cultures), sometimes indefinite suppression if bone not resected
Strict glucose control, offloading with total contact cast after acute infection controlled
Multidisciplinary diabetic foot team: endocrinology, vascular surgery, podiatry, infectious disease
pitfalls: Diabetic foot ulcers have high morbidity: 25% diabetics develop foot ulcer, 20% of those need amputation
Probe-to-bone test: >90% specificity for osteomyelitis if positive
Gas in soft tissues (crepitus on exam or X-ray) indicates necrotizing infection - urgent surgical emergency
Revascularization BEFORE amputation improves healing and may allow more distal amputation preserving function
Prevention is key: daily foot inspection, proper footwear, regular podiatry care, tight glucose control

cases.title: Woman with Sudden Vision Loss
learning_objectives: Recognize signs and symptoms of retinal artery occlusion
Understand emergent management of central retinal artery occlusion
Differentiate arterial from venous retinal occlusions
cases.presentation: 68-year-old woman with sudden painless loss of vision in right eye 2 hours ago

history.chief_complaint: Suddenly went blind in my right eye
history.hpi: Patient was reading when she suddenly lost all vision in her right eye. No pain, no trauma, no flashing lights or floaters beforehand. Vision loss was immediate and complete. Had episode of transient vision loss in same eye last week that resolved after 5 minutes (amaurosis fugax). No headache, jaw claudication, or scalp tenderness.
history.pmh: Hypertension, hyperlipidemia, atrial fibrillation (not on anticoagulation), prior TIA 3 years ago
history.social: Non-smoker, occasional alcohol, retired teacher

physical_exam.vitals: BP 165/92, HR 88 irregular, RR 16, O2 98% RA, Temp 98.2°F
physical_exam.eye_exam: Right eye: no light perception, afferent pupillary defect (Marcus Gunn pupil), fundoscopy shows pale retina with cherry-red spot at macula, boxcar segmentation of blood in retinal arteries. Left eye: 20/30 vision, normal exam
physical_exam.neuro: Alert and oriented, no other focal deficits

labs.esr: 12 mm/hr (normal - rules out giant cell arteritis)

imaging.echocardiogram: Enlarged left atrium, no visible thrombus, EF 55%

cases.explanation: Central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO) is an ophthalmologic emergency - the 'stroke of the eye'. Key features: (1) Sudden, painless, complete vision loss, (2) Afferent pupillary defect (APD), (3) Cherry-red spot at fovea with pale surrounding retina (retinal edema), (4) Boxcar segmentation of blood column, (5) Prior amaurosis fugax (TIA of eye), (6) Risk factors: AFib not anticoagulated, carotid stenosis, prior TIA. Visual prognosis is poor - retinal survival only 90 minutes without blood flow. This is a stroke equivalent requiring same urgent workup.
management_pearls: EMERGENT ophthalmology consult - this is time-sensitive (ideally <4 hours)
Ocular massage: firm pressure on closed eye for 5 seconds, release for 5 seconds, repeat x5 (may dislodge embolus)
Lower intraocular pressure: acetazolamide 500mg IV, timolol drops, anterior chamber paracentesis by ophthalmology
Hyperbaric oxygen if available within 24 hours
Start anticoagulation (heparin) if cardioembolic source and no contraindications
Stroke workup: carotid imaging, echocardiogram, telemetry
ESR/CRP to rule out giant cell arteritis (treat empirically with steroids if suspected)
pitfalls: Window for treatment is narrow - retinal ischemia time even shorter than brain (90 min vs 4.5 hours)
Branch retinal artery occlusion: sectoral vision loss, better prognosis than CRAO
Giant cell arteritis must be excluded in patients >50 - check ESR/CRP, start steroids if suspicious
Amaurosis fugax is TIA - requires same urgent stroke workup and prevention

physical_exam.general: In severe distress, crying, holding groin
physical_exam.genitourinary: Left testicle: high-riding, horizontal lie (bell-clapper deformity), exquisitely tender, swollen, firm. Absent cremasteric reflex on left. Right testicle: normal position, non-tender. No scrotal erythema or warmth. Negative Prehn's sign (no relief with elevation).

imaging.doppler_ultrasound: Decreased arterial flow to left testicle compared to right, heterogeneous echotexture

cases.explanation: Testicular torsion is a urologic emergency requiring surgery within 6 hours to save the testicle. Key features: (1) Sudden severe unilateral testicular pain, (2) High-riding testicle with horizontal lie, (3) Absent cremasteric reflex (95% sensitive), (4) Negative Prehn's sign (pain not relieved by elevation), (5) Peak age 12-18 years, (6) Often occurs during sleep. This is a CLINICAL diagnosis - do not delay surgery for imaging if high suspicion. Salvage rate: >90% if <6 hours, <50% if 12-24 hours, <10% if >24 hours.
management_pearls: URGENT urology consult - do not delay for imaging if high clinical suspicion
Manual detorsion can be attempted: 'open the book' - rotate affected testicle outward (medial to lateral)
Definitive treatment: surgical exploration with detorsion and bilateral orchiopexy
If testicle non-viable at surgery: orchiectomy of affected side, orchiopexy of contralateral side (prevent future torsion)
NPO, IV access, analgesia while awaiting surgery
Time is testicle: <6 hours for best salvage
pitfalls: Never delay surgery for imaging if clinical suspicion is high - torsion is a clinical diagnosis
Absent cremasteric reflex is 99% specific for torsion
Intermittent torsion-detorsion can present with recurrent pain - still needs prophylactic bilateral orchiopexy
Epididymitis: gradual onset, fever, positive Prehn's sign, cremasteric reflex present, pyuria, more common >20 years

history.hpi: Patient reports progressive severe itching starting 2 weeks ago, worse at night, primarily affecting palms and soles but now entire body. No relief with moisturizers or antihistamines. No rash. Sleep severely disrupted. Denies jaundice, dark urine, or light stools. This is her second pregnancy - had similar symptoms with first pregnancy at 36 weeks.
history.ob_history: G2P1, first pregnancy complicated by cholestasis of pregnancy, delivered at 37 weeks, baby healthy
history.social: Married, works as accountant, non-smoker

physical_exam.general: Appears tired, multiple excoriations on arms and legs from scratching

cases.explanation: Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy (ICP) typically presents in third trimester with severe pruritus, especially palms and soles, worse at night. Key features: (1) Intense pruritus without primary rash, (2) Elevated bile acids >10 μmol/L (diagnosis confirmed), (3) Elevated transaminases, (4) History of ICP in prior pregnancy (45-70% recurrence), (5) Family history common. ICP poses significant fetal risks: increased stillbirth (1-2%), preterm delivery, meconium passage. Most concerning when bile acids >40 μmol/L.
management_pearls: Ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) 10-15 mg/kg/day divided BID-TID - improves pruritus and bile acids
Cholestyramine 4g TID-QID (second-line) - may worsen fat-soluble vitamin absorption
Antihistamines for symptomatic relief (limited efficacy but safe)
Twice-weekly NST and weekly bile acid monitoring
Delivery at 36-37 weeks to reduce stillbirth risk (earlier if bile acids >100)
Vitamin K supplementation if bile acids very high or prolonged PT
Symptoms resolve rapidly postpartum (usually within 48 hours)
pitfalls: Bile acids are diagnostic test - LFTs can be normal in ICP
Stillbirth can occur suddenly even with reassuring fetal testing
Postpartum hemorrhage risk increased due to vitamin K malabsorption
Increased risk of gestational diabetes, preeclampsia, and recurrence in future pregnancies
Women with ICP have increased risk of future hepatobiliary disease

history.chief_complaint: Can't speak clearly and right side is weak
history.hpi: Per wife, patient was eating breakfast when he suddenly dropped his fork and his speech became slurred. Right arm became weak and drooped. Called 911 immediately. Last known well time was 7:30 AM (now 9:00 AM = 90 minutes). No headache, no seizures, no loss of consciousness. Wife reports he has been compliant with medications.
history.pmh: Hypertension, hyperlipidemia, atrial fibrillation on warfarin, prior TIA 2 years ago
history.social: Retired engineer, non-smoker, occasional alcohol

physical_exam.vitals: BP 178/95, HR 88 irregular, RR 16, O2 97% RA, Temp 98.4°F, glucose 125
physical_exam.neuro: NIH Stroke Scale 12. Alert, severe expressive aphasia (Broca's), follows some commands. Right facial droop. Right arm 3/5 strength (drifts down), right leg 4/5, left side 5/5. Right pronator drift. Decreased sensation on right. Gaze preference to left. No neglect.

imaging.ct_head_noncontrast: No hemorrhage, no early signs of infarct, no mass effect
imaging.cta_head_neck: Left M1 MCA occlusion, good collaterals

cases.explanation: Acute ischemic stroke with left MCA territory involvement causing right hemiparesis and expressive aphasia. Key features: (1) Sudden onset focal neurologic deficit, (2) Clear last known well time (90 minutes - within tPA window), (3) Risk factors: AFib with subtherapeutic INR, HTN, prior TIA, (4) NIH Stroke Scale 12 (moderate-severe stroke), (5) Large vessel occlusion (M1 MCA) on CTA, (6) Favorable penumbra on CT perfusion (candidate for thrombectomy). This is CODE STROKE - time is brain!
management_pearls: tPA (alteplase) 0.9 mg/kg (max 90mg): 10% bolus, 90% over 1 hour - if <4.5 hours from LKW and no contraindications
tPA contraindications here: INR 1.8 (>1.7 is contraindication) - consider reversal vs proceed to thrombectomy
EMERGENT thrombectomy consult - LVO with favorable perfusion, within 24-hour window
BP management: permissive hypertension if not giving tPA (goal <220/120), lower to <185/110 if giving tPA
Aspirin 325mg at 24 hours after tPA (or immediately if no tPA given)
Admit to stroke unit, frequent neuro checks, DVT prophylaxis (pneumatic compression), dysphagia screening
pitfalls: Door-to-needle time for tPA should be <60 minutes - don't delay for detailed history
INR >1.7 is contraindication for tPA but may still get thrombectomy
Stroke mimics (5-30% of suspected strokes): seizure, hypoglycemia, migraine, conversion disorder - but 'treat first, ask questions later'
Large vessel occlusions benefit most from thrombectomy - extended window up to 24 hours with favorable perfusion imaging

cases.title: Young Adult with Bloody Diarrhea and Abdominal Pain

Understand difference between UC and Crohn's disease
Apply severity assessment for inflammatory bowel disease
cases.presentation: 23-year-old woman with 8 weeks of bloody diarrhea, urgency, and crampy abdominal pain

history.chief_complaint: Blood in my stool for 2 months, going to bathroom 10+ times a day
history.hpi: Patient reports gradual onset of diarrhea 8 weeks ago, initially 4-5 bowel movements daily, now 10-12 times per day. Stools are loose with visible bright red blood and mucus. Associated with crampy lower abdominal pain, relieved temporarily by bowel movements. Urgency and tenesmus. 15-pound weight loss. Fatigue. Occasional low-grade fever. No nausea or vomiting. Tried over-the-counter anti-diarrheals with no improvement.
history.social: Graduate student, non-smoker, occasional alcohol, no recent travel

physical_exam.abdomen: Soft, diffuse lower abdominal tenderness, no rebound or guarding, hyperactive bowel sounds, no masses
physical_exam.rectal: Bright red blood on glove, no external hemorrhoids or fissures
physical_exam.skin: No rash, no erythema nodosum, no pyoderma gangrenosum

labs.stool_studies: Negative for C. diff, Salmonella, Shigella, Campylobacter, ova and parasites

imaging.colonoscopy: Continuous inflammation from rectum to splenic flexure with loss of vascular pattern, friability, spontaneous bleeding, and pseudopolyps. Normal terminal ileum. Biopsies show chronic inflammation with crypt abscesses and distortion, no granulomas.

cases.explanation: Ulcerative colitis (UC) is an inflammatory bowel disease causing continuous mucosal inflammation of the colon. Key features: (1) Chronic bloody diarrhea with urgency and tenesmus, (2) Continuous inflammation starting from rectum extending proximally (left-sided colitis in this case), (3) Friable mucosa with loss of vascular pattern and pseudopolyps, (4) Crypt abscesses on histology, NO granulomas (differentiates from Crohn's), (5) Elevated inflammatory markers, anemia, thrombocytosis, (6) Family history of IBD. This is moderate severity UC (10-12 stools/day, anemia, elevated ESR/CRP).
management_pearls: Severity assessment: Mild (<4 stools/day, no systemic signs), Moderate (4-6 stools/day), Severe (>6 stools/day with systemic toxicity)
Induction therapy: 5-ASA (mesalamine) for mild-moderate, corticosteroids (prednisone 40-60mg daily) for moderate-severe
This patient needs: Prednisone + mesalamine for induction, taper steroids over 8-12 weeks
Steroid-dependent or refractory: biologics (anti-TNF like infliximab, vedolizumab, or JAK inhibitors)
Maintenance: mesalamine indefinitely, immunomodulators (azathioprine) or biologics if needed
Monitor for complications: toxic megacolon, perforation, colorectal cancer (screening colonoscopy every 1-2 years after 8-10 years of disease)
pitfalls: UC vs Crohn's: UC is continuous from rectum, mucosal only, no granulomas, bloody diarrhea. Crohn's is skip lesions, transmural, granulomas, can affect any GI tract location, less bloody diarrhea
Always rule out infectious causes before starting immunosuppression - check stool studies and C. diff
Toxic megacolon: acute colonic dilation >6cm with systemic toxicity - surgical emergency
NSAIDs can trigger or worsen IBD flares

cases.title: Child with Limp and Hip Pain
learning_objectives: Recognize transient synovitis vs septic arthritis
Apply Kocher criteria for risk stratification
cases.presentation: 5-year-old boy with right hip pain and refusal to bear weight for 2 days

history.chief_complaint: Won't walk on right leg, says hip hurts
history.hpi: Mother reports child developed right hip pain 2 days ago and has been limping. Today refuses to walk or bear weight on right leg. Pain is worse with movement. Had upper respiratory infection last week that resolved. Low-grade fever yesterday (100.5°F at home). No trauma. Child is otherwise acting normally, eating and drinking well.
history.pmh: Healthy, up to date on immunizations
history.social: Kindergarten student, lives with parents and siblings

physical_exam.general: Alert, playful but guarding right leg
physical_exam.gait: Antalgic gait, refuses to bear full weight on right
physical_exam.hip_exam: Right hip: limited range of motion (especially internal rotation), pain with passive range of motion, hip held in slight flexion and external rotation. No erythema or warmth. Left hip: normal ROM, non-tender.
physical_exam.neuro: Normal strength, sensation, reflexes in both legs

imaging.hip_xray: Normal joint space, no effusion visible, no fracture, femoral head appears normal

cases.explanation: Transient synovitis (toxic synovitis) is the most common cause of acute hip pain in children 3-8 years old. Key features: (1) Recent viral URI (classic trigger), (2) Gradual onset hip pain and limp, (3) Low-grade or no fever (<101.3°F), (4) Limited ROM especially internal rotation, (5) Small joint effusion on ultrasound, (6) Normal or mildly elevated inflammatory markers. Kocher criteria score 1/4 (fever >101.5°F, non-weight bearing, ESR >40, WBC >12) - low probability of septic arthritis (<3%). If score ≥3, high risk septic arthritis - needs joint aspiration.
management_pearls: Kocher criteria for septic arthritis: 1 point each for: fever >101.5°F, refusal to bear weight, ESR >40, WBC >12,000. Score 0-1: <3% risk, Score 2: 40% risk, Score 3: 93% risk, Score 4: 99% risk
This patient (score 1): likely transient synovitis - can manage conservatively with close follow-up
Treatment: NSAIDs (ibuprofen 10mg/kg Q6H), rest, close follow-up in 24-48 hours
If Kocher ≥2 or high clinical suspicion: joint aspiration (cell count, Gram stain, culture)
Septic arthritis synovial fluid: WBC >50,000 (often >80,000), >75-90% PMNs, positive Gram stain/culture
Resolution typically within 1-2 weeks. Recurrence common (4-17%).
pitfalls: Septic arthritis is a surgical emergency - can destroy joint in 24-48 hours. When in doubt, aspirate.
Bilateral hip involvement makes septic arthritis less likely but doesn't rule it out
Legg-Calvé-Perthes: boys 4-8yo, insidious onset, X-ray shows femoral head changes later (initially normal)
SCFE: obese adolescents 10-16yo, hip held in external rotation, X-ray shows femoral head displacement
If child is systemically ill, toxic-appearing, high fever, or rapidly worsening - assume septic arthritis until proven otherwise

Understand management of acute upper GI bleeding in cirrhosis

cases.presentation: 52-year-old man with cirrhosis presenting with massive hematemesis and altered mental status

history.chief_complaint: Vomiting large amounts of blood
history.hpi: Per EMS, patient found by roommate vomiting bright red blood. Multiple episodes of large-volume hematemesis. Patient confused and disoriented. History of alcohol use disorder with known cirrhosis. Non-compliant with medications. Recent increase in abdominal girth. No prior variceal bleeding. Roommate reports he has been drinking heavily this past month.
history.pmh: Alcoholic cirrhosis (Child-Pugh B), esophageal varices (seen on EGD 1 year ago), ascites, portal hypertension
history.medications: Supposed to be on: nadolol, lactulose, furosemide, spironolactone (not taking consistently)
history.social: Alcohol use disorder (1 pint vodka daily x 20 years), unemployed, lives with roommate

physical_exam.general: Pale, diaphoretic, confused (GCS 13), blood around mouth
physical_exam.heent: Conjunctival pallor, scleral icterus, blood in oropharynx
physical_exam.abdomen: Distended with shifting dullness (ascites), hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, caput medusae, no tenderness or rigidity
physical_exam.neuro: Confused, asterixis present (hepatic encephalopathy)

imaging.cxr: No aspiration, small bilateral pleural effusions

cases.explanation: Acute variceal hemorrhage in decompensated cirrhosis - life-threatening emergency with 20-30% mortality. Key features: (1) Known cirrhosis with portal hypertension, (2) Massive hematemesis with hemodynamic instability, (3) Signs of chronic liver disease: ascites, jaundice, encephalopathy, coagulopathy, thrombocytopenia, (4) Child-Pugh B-C cirrhosis at highest risk. Esophageal varices are the source in 50-70% of upper GI bleeds in cirrhotics. Risk factors for variceal bleeding: large varices, red wale marks, Child-Pugh C, active alcohol use.
management_pearls: RESUSCITATION: 2 large-bore IVs, blood bank activation (type and cross 6 units), crystalloid cautiously (avoid over-resuscitation - increases portal pressure)
Target hemoglobin 7-8 g/dL (restrictive transfusion - over-transfusion worsens bleeding)
Octreotide 50 mcg bolus then 50 mcg/hr infusion x 2-5 days (splanchnic vasoconstriction, decreases portal pressure)
Antibiotics: ceftriaxone 1g daily (or ciprofloxacin) - reduces mortality, prevents SBP
URGENT EGD within 12 hours (ideally within 6 hours) for diagnosis and treatment: variceal band ligation or sclerotherapy
Correct coagulopathy cautiously: goal platelets >50,000, INR correction controversial (may worsen portal pressure)
Proton pump inhibitor: pantoprazole 80mg bolus then 8mg/hr (if non-variceal source)
Airway protection: intubate before EGD if obtunded or massive hematemesis (aspiration risk)
Balloon tamponade (Blakemore tube) if refractory bleeding - temporizing bridge to TIPS
TIPS (transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt) if refractory to medical/endoscopic therapy
pitfalls: Over-resuscitation increases portal pressure and worsens bleeding - target SBP 90-100
Always start octreotide before EGD - improves hemostasis and facilitates procedure
Antibiotics are mandatory - infection occurs in 20% and increases mortality
Fresh frozen plasma does not reliably correct INR in cirrhosis and may worsen volume overload
Balloon tamponade: high complication rate (aspiration, esophageal rupture) - use only as bridge to definitive therapy
